verses.translation_literal: In the going out of Israel from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people speaking in a foreign tongue,
verses.translation_dramatic: When Israel walked out of Egypt, when the house of Jacob came away from a people whose speech was a stranger's, whose words fell on the ear like noise,
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a sentence that does not finish. It is a temporal clause, 'when Israel went out', and it hangs in the air until verse 2 supplies the main verb, so the performer should hold the breath and let the audience wait. The first colon uses 'Israel', the second 'the house of Jacob': a pair of names for one people, the tribe's later name and its ancestor's, and Malbim's note that 'Jacob' means the common crowd and 'Israel' the elite is a late distinction, not a requirement of the Hebrew.

The rare word is לֹעֵז, a participle of לָעַז, a root that occurs only here in the Bible. Its meaning is fixed by later Hebrew, where לועז means 'foreign language', and by Rashi, who ties it to the language that is not the holy tongue. The KJV's 'strange language' is not wrong, but 'strange' in 1611 meant 'foreign'; modern readers hear 'odd'. The point is not that Egyptian is peculiar. It is that the slaves lived among people whose words they could not simply share, and that leaving Egypt was leaving a world with another speech. Radak argues, with a good sense of history, that this cannot mean total incomprehension: the Hebrews had lived there many years, and some surely understood Egyptian, since they served among the Egyptians, while at home in Goshen they spoke their own language. So the phrase marks alien allegiance and alien rule, not a literal wall of sound. The tone here should be quiet, almost wondering, and the departure, not the oppression, is the subject.

philological_notes.note: A participle of a root found only here in the Hebrew Bible: 'one who speaks a foreign, unintelligible tongue'. Later Hebrew uses לועז for any language other than Hebrew (and the related word לעז for a foreign-language gloss). Rashi compares Isaiah 33:19, where the people 'of obscure speech' appears, linking it to נועז by an interchange of nun and lamed.

'The house of Jacob' is a household metaphor for the whole nation as one family descended from one man. It parallels 'Israel' in the first colon as a synonym; the verse repeats the sense rather than adding a new group.

verses.translation_literal: Judah became his holy place, Israel his dominions.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Judah became His holy place, and Israel His realm, the whole land under His rule.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the main verb the psalm withheld, and with it a surprise: the subject is not Israel, who left, but Judah and Israel together, and the one who owns them is only 'his', never named. God is the unspoken he of the psalm until verse 7, so do not speak the name; let the pronoun carry the weight.

Three things are worth knowing. First, 'Judah' and 'Israel' appear as a pair, as in the later division of the kingdoms; a hearer in the monarchy or after the exile would feel both halves of the nation in the line, and the psalm reads as a poem about the people as a whole, not about a particular tribe. Ibn Ezra explains the feminine verb: Judah here is the community, not the man. Second, לְקָדְשׁוֹ is 'his holiness' (the noun קֹדֶשׁ), whether a holy place, a holy thing, or a holy people: the KJV's 'sanctuary' narrows it to a building, and the traditions disagree. Radak reads it as the people taken out of an unclean nation and made holy; the Targum reads the 'assembly of the house of Judah'. Third, the plural of מַמְשְׁלוֹתָיו, 'his dominions', is a plural of extent or majesty, and Meiri notes its unusual pointing. The rabbis in Rashi and Radak add the story that Nachshon of Judah leapt into the sea first. That is a midrash, a good one for a reader, but the psalm does not say it. The psalm says only that God, not Pharaoh, now held title to this people.

philological_notes.note: 'For his holiness', from קֹדֶשׁ: an abstract noun, a holy place or a holy people, with the preposition ל marking the thing the subject became. The KJV 'sanctuary' is one possibility, 'holy place' another; both fit the parallel with 'dominions'.
A plural noun meaning 'rule' or 'realm' (מֶמְשָׁלָה), here 'his dominions'. The plural may express extent or fullness of rule; it parallels 'holy place'.

token_glosses.gloss: for his holiness, his holy place

verses.translation_literal: The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turns to backward.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sea saw, and ran. The Jordan turned and went back the way it had come.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar of this verse is where the story lives. The sea 'saw', and the verb has no object: the KJV adds 'it', which gives a ghost a thing to see. The Hebrew says only that the sea saw, and the actor must decide what that look contains. Then comes 'and it fled', the same verb (נוס) that is used of an army routed on a battlefield. The sea is a soldier who breaks and runs. The commentators say this at once: Radak and Meiri call it a figure, as though the sea were afraid; Metzudat David says the sea saw Israel entering and ran from its place, leaving dry ground.

The tenses shift. The first colon is narrative (past), and the second is imperfect: 'the Jordan turns back'. Whether that means a habitual fact or a continuing event, the psalm joins two crossings into one moment. The Red Sea belongs to the exodus, the Jordan to Joshua, and a first audience would hear that the one God has made the same river-crossing twice in a different place. Tradition (Rashi) went further and said that all the primordial waters of creation were split. 'Sea' (יָם) was also the name of a god in the Canaanite poems of Ugarit, who fought Baal; to a Syrian or Canaanite ear a sea that sees and flees would be a god defeated, a stinging joke, but the psalm itself says nothing about that. Say the lines flat and fast, like news.

philological_notes.note: 'And it fled', the standard verb for fleeing in battle. The sea is pictured as an enemy that breaks and runs before an approaching force.
'It turns to the rear'. The verb סבב means to go round or turn, here a river reversing, and אחור is 'back, behind'. The same phrase returns in verse 5.

verses.translation_literal: The mountains skipped like rams, hills like sons of the flock.
verses.translation_dramatic: The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs at play.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the earth itself moves, and the verb is a lively one: רָקַד, 'skip, dance', the word for the leaping of animals and children. In form the image is joyful: the heaviest things in the landscape are made light, and that is the poem's best joke. But the commentators in the packet hear fear inside the play. Ibn Ezra says the mountains shook before the glory of God, Radak that they 'trembled and quaked', and Metzudat David that they leapt 'for the greatness of the dread' at the giving of the Torah. Verse 7 settles it with 'tremble'. So the performer has two things to hold at once: the caper of a flock, and the shudder of a mountain. The leap is the shape; the terror, if you take the commentators' reading, is the cause.

The KJV's 'little hills like lambs' is nearly right but adds 'little', which the Hebrew leaves out and only implies by contrast with 'mountains'; the literal 'sons of the flock' (בְּנֵי־צֹאן) is the family word for the young of sheep and goats. 'Ram' (אַיִל) is a full-grown, horned male, so the mountains are big animals and the hills their young. The second colon omits the verb and borrows it from the first, a pattern the psalm repeats in verse 6. Tradition ties the image to Sinai: Meiri quotes Exodus 19:18, 'all the mountain trembled greatly'. The psalm itself does not name the place. A shepherd's audience knew the sight of a flock bounding at the pen-gate. Play it with a smile that does not last.

philological_notes.note: 'They skipped, danced': a verb of lively leaping, used of animals and children, so the image is joyful in form. The commentators nonetheless read the leaping as quaking in dread (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David), and verse 7 answers it with 'tremble'. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'leapt'.
Literally 'sons of the flock', that is, lambs and kids. The KJV's 'lambs' is correct in sense; the Hebrew keeps the family word 'sons', which echoes 'house of Jacob' in verse 1.

verses.translation_literal: What [is] to you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, [that] you turn to backward?
verses.translation_dramatic: What is the matter with you, sea, that you run? Jordan, why do you turn and go back?
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Until now a narrator told the story in the third person; now the poet turns and speaks to the sea and the river, and the voice rises. 'What is it to you' (מַה־לְּךָ) is the idiom for 'what ails you?', 'what is the matter with you?', and the KJV's 'what ailed thee' is one of the places where its antique English is accurate. But note the tense: the verbs here are imperfect, and the question is asked as if the sea were still running as we speak. The psalm puts the audience at the shore.

Radak and Meiri both say the question is asked to draw out the answer, which arrives at once in verse 7. This is a catechism, a question set so that the right answer can be given: the sea does not flee by chance. Metzudat David says that the poet speaks to the sea as though it could reply. The sea and Jordan are the poet's interlocutors, and the effect is of a poet who has stepped out of the line of history and into the scene. Speak this verse as one speaks to a startled animal, then wait.

philological_notes.note: An idiom: 'what [is] to you?', 'what ails you?', 'what is wrong?' (compare Genesis 21:17 and Isaiah 22:1, not in the packet). It is a question asked of one who acts strangely.
Imperfect, second person: 'that you flee' or 'keep fleeing'. It echoes the narrative 'and it fled' in verse 3 but now as direct address.

verses.translation_literal: [What is to you,] O mountains, [that] you skip like rams, O hills, like sons of the flock?
verses.translation_dramatic: And you, mountains, what makes you leap like rams? And you, hills, like lambs?
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse repeats verse 4 almost word for word, and the only change is the grammar: the verb becomes second person, and the mountains are now spoken to. The poet applies the sea-and-river question to the mountains and hills in a second panel, matching the pair of verse 3 and the pair of verse 4 with the pair of verse 5 and this one. The pattern is a kind of double mirror, narrative then address, and the audience should hear the echo as an echo.

The five English versions split here because the Hebrew has no question word. The KJV and ASV treat 'that ye skipped' as a clause hanging on an unwritten 'what ailed you'; YLT and the Webster text differ in tense; the BBE asks 'why'. The Hebrew can be read as a statement (an exclamation of wonder: 'you mountains, you skip like rams!'), but every medieval commentator in the packet carries the question forward. Metzudat David spells it out: 'what is to you, mountains, that you skip?' I keep the question in brackets in the literal layer and make it explicit in the dramatic one. Play it with a lighter touch than verse 5: the sea fled in fear, but the hills only frolic, and the joke is the same joke twice.

philological_notes.note: Imperfect second person plural, 'you skip', matching the perfect 'they skipped' of verse 4. The change of person is the only difference between the two verses.

verses.translation_literal: From before the Lord, writhe, O earth, from before the God of Jacob,
verses.translation_dramatic: Tremble, earth, tremble before the Lord, before the God of Jacob,
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer comes, and it is not an explanation but a command: the poet does not say 'they fled because...', he tells the earth to shake. God is named here for the first time in the psalm, and by the title אָדוֹן, 'lord, master', not the divine name. The KJV prints 'Lord' for אָדוֹן in a way that is easy to confuse with its 'LORD' for the name; here it is a title, a master before whom a slave trembles. Radak says exactly that: the answer 'from before the Lord' is that of 'a servant who is afraid and shakes before his master' (on 114:5). Given a psalm that begins with a people leaving slavery, the word is pointed: the people have a new master.

The form חוּלִי is the puzzle of the verse. The simplest reading, Ibn Ezra's and Meiri's, is a feminine imperative of חוּל, 'writhe, shake, dance in labour', addressed to 'earth' (feminine); Ibn Ezra compares it to קומי, 'arise!'. Radak reads it as an infinitive with a pronoun, 'my trembling and my fear', spoken by the earth itself, and Meiri reports that reading as the view of others. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as a participle of חלל, 'the one who forms or gives birth to the earth', with a superfluous yod, like the endings in 113:5–6 and 114:8. All of them reach much the same effect: the earth is shaken before its maker. The root also serves for a woman in labour, so the trembling earth may be giving birth; keep the double sense in the voice. 'Before the God of Jacob' ties back to 'the house of Jacob' in verse 1 and closes the frame: the God who owns the earth is the God of this one family. Radak adds that he bought this family out of the house of slaves by his strength, so the sea and Jordan have every reason to give way.

philological_notes.note: Most likely a feminine singular imperative of חוּל, 'writhe, tremble' (also used of labour pains), addressed to the earth (אָרֶץ, feminine); so Ibn Ezra, and Meiri. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as a participle of חלל, 'the one who forms or gives birth to the earth', with a superfluous yod. Radak reads it as an infinitive with a pronoun, 'my trembling', spoken by the earth; Meiri mentions this as the view of others.
'Lord, master': a title, not the divine name. Radak ties it to a servant who shakes before his master, and so connects it to the ownership language of verse 2.
A singular, poetic form of 'God' (Eloah), common in the Psalms and Job in place of the plural Elohim; here it stands in construct with Jacob.

verses.translation_literal: The one who turns the rock [into] a pool of water, flint [into] a spring of water.
verses.translation_dramatic: He who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on its last reversal, and it is a different kind of reversal from the earlier ones. The sea, the river and the hills moved at once; here God is named by what he is always doing: הַהֹפְכִי, 'the one who turns'. The participle with the article is an epithet, not a past tense, and the KJV's 'which turned' makes it a single event, a miracle in the history books. In the Hebrew it is a title of God, who makes dry things wet and hard things soft.

The verb is the key to the whole psalm. 'Turn' (הפך) echoes the 'turning back' (סבב) of the Jordan, and the verse enacts what the earlier verses reported. And look at what is turned: צוּר, 'rock', one of the commonest Hebrew words for God himself, becomes a pond; חַלָּמִישׁ, 'flint', hard rock, a spring. Metzudat Zion defines חַלָּמִישׁ as hard rock and illustrates it with 'oil from the flint rock' (Deuteronomy 32:13). The image is of the desert, where a pool and a spring were life; Meiri, commenting on verse 4, ties it to the rock that was struck so that waters flowed (Psalm 78:15–20). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion remark that the final vav in 'his spring' is an extra letter, and Rashi and Metzudat Zion say the same of the yod in 'who turns'; I do not translate them. Radak draws the lesson: the one who can turn the wet sea into dry land can turn dry rock to water, for he is lord and creator of all. The sense is that the God who commands the earth to shake is the one who makes it give. Let the voice drop and soften on the last word, 'water': the poem ends not with terror but with a drink.

philological_notes.note: A participle with the article, 'the one who turns', with an extra yod, which Rashi and Metzudat Zion mark as superfluous, as in 113:5–6. A timeless epithet, not a past tense.
'A pool of water': אֲגַם is a marsh, a pool or a gathering place of water. Metzudat Zion defines it as the place where water enters.
'Flint' or very hard rock. Metzudat Zion defines it as hard rock (סלע קשה) and illustrates it with Deuteronomy 32:13, 'oil from the flint rock'. Meiri glosses it simply as 'rock'.
